title: React Apps: Forms, Effects and Data
summary: Build real apps with React: show and hide things, handle forms, load data, share state between components, and finish with a project.
objectives: Show, hide and switch parts of the page with conditional rendering
Build forms whose fields are controlled by state
Load data from a server with useEffect and fetch
Share state between components by lifting it up
Plan and build a complete app from components

lessons.title: Show and hide things
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Sometimes yes, sometimes no Lots of things on a page only appear sometimes: a "You win!" message, a menu that opens, a warning. In React you decide with a bit of JavaScript right inside the JSX. ### && means "only if" ```jsx {isOpen &&

The shop is open!

} ``` Read it as: "if `isOpen` is true, show the paragraph." If it's false, React shows nothing at all. ### ? : means "this or that" ```jsx

{isOpen ? "Come in!" : "Sorry, we're closed."}

``` Read it as: "is it open? If yes, the first thing. If not, the second thing." This is called the **ternary**. Use it when you always want to show *something*, just a different thing. ### Flip it with ! `!` means "not", so `!true` is `false`. That makes a toggle button easy: ```jsx ``` ### New words - **Conditional rendering**: showing something on the page only when a condition is true. - **&&**: "and". In JSX, `{x &&

}` shows the paragraph only when `x` is true. - **Ternary** (`? :`): picks one of two things: `condition ? ifYes : ifNo`. - **! (not)**: flips true to false, and false to true.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: Press the button to switch the light. The emoji and the words use the ternary; the "Too bright!" warning uses `&&`.

lessons.title: Conditional rendering
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## UI that depends on state Most screens have parts that come and go: a spinner while loading, an error after a failed save, a "Next" button after you answer. Since a component is just a function, you choose what to return with ordinary JavaScript. ### Three tools **`&&`**: render something or nothing. ```jsx {unread > 0 && {unread}} ``` **Ternary `? :`**: render one thing or another. Works for whole elements, text and attributes: ```jsx {loggedIn ? : }
  • …
    • ``` **`if` before the return**: for bigger decisions, or to return early. ```jsx function Profile({ user }) { if (!user) return

    Loading…

    ; return

    {user.name}

    ; } ``` A component may also `return null` to render nothing. ### The 0 gotcha `&&` returns its left side when that side is falsy, and React renders numbers. So `{items.length && }` shows a stray **0** when the list is empty. Make the left side a real boolean: `{items.length > 0 && }`. ### Derive conditions from state Store the minimal state (here: which option was picked) and compute the rest during render: `const answered = picked !== null;`. Named conditions also make the JSX read like a sentence: `{answered && !correct && }`. ### New words - **Conditional rendering**: choosing what a component renders based on state or props. - **Falsy**: values that count as false in a condition: `false`, `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. - **Ternary operator**: `condition ? a : b`, an expression that picks one of two values. - **Early return**: returning from a function before the end, often for a special case. - **null**: "no value". A component that returns `null` renders nothing.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: The badge only appears when there are unread messages (using `> 0`, so no stray 0), the list switches to a friendly message when it's empty, and the class changes for read messages.

lessons.title: Typing and forms
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Boxes that React can read To use what someone types, keep it in **state**. Then connect the text box to that state with two props: ```jsx const [name, setName] = useState(""); setName(event.target.value)} /> ``` - `value={name}` shows whatever is in state. - `onChange` runs every time a key is pressed. `event.target.value` is the text in the box, so we save it with `setName`. Now `name` is always up to date, and you can use it anywhere: `

Hello, {name}!

` changes as you type! ### Forms Put the box and a button inside a `
`. When the button is clicked (or Enter is pressed), the form's `onSubmit` runs: ```jsx function handleSubmit(event) { event.preventDefault(); // do something with name } ...
``` `event.preventDefault()` stops the browser's old habit of reloading the page when a form is sent. ### New words - **onChange**: runs your code every time the text in a box changes. - **event.target.value**: the text that's in the box right now. - **onSubmit**: runs your code when a form is sent. - **preventDefault**: tells the browser not to do its usual thing (for a form, reloading the page).
lessons.exampleMarkdown: Type in the box: the big text copies you as you type, because both use the same `word` state. Press **Shout!** to save it.

lessons.title: Controlled forms
lessons.learnMarkdown: ## One source of truth An `` keeps its own value in the DOM. In React you usually take control of it: the value lives in **state**, the input shows that state, and every keystroke updates the state. That's a **controlled component**: ```jsx const [email, setEmail] = useState(""); setEmail(e.target.value)} /> ``` The state is the **single source of truth**. Because you always have the current value, you can validate as the user types, disable a button until a field is filled in, or clear the form with `setEmail("")`. The same pattern works for every field. Only the property you read changes: | Field | Prop | Read it from | | --- | --- | --- | | ``, `
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A sign-up form with three controlled fields. The button is disabled until the form is valid, which is easy because every value is already in state.

lessons.title: Getting data with useEffect
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Asking the internet for data Remember `fetch` from the JavaScript course? It asks a server for data. In React, there's one more question: **when** should the component ask? Not every time it draws (that would ask over and over!), just once, when it first shows up. That's what `useEffect` is for: ```jsx useEffect(() => { fetch("https://api.codegrove.test/pets") .then((response) => response.json()) .then((data) => setPets(data)); }, []); ``` - The code inside runs **after** the component appears on the page. - The `[]` at the end means "only run this once." Don't forget it! - When the data arrives, `setPets` saves it in state, and React draws the list. ### While you wait Data takes a moment to arrive. Until then, the list is empty, so it's polite to say so: ```jsx {pets.length === 0 &&

Loading…

} ``` The practice server in the preview lives at `https://api.codegrove.test`. It has `/planets`, `/pets` and `/weather`. ### New words - **useEffect**: a React tool for running code after the component shows up, like fetching data. - **Effect**: work that reaches outside the component, like talking to a server. - **[] (dependency array)**: the list at the end of useEffect. Empty means "run once."
lessons.exampleMarkdown: The effect runs once, after the page appears. It fetches the weather, saves it in state, and React draws it. Until then, the `weather` state is `null`, so we show **Loading…**.

lessons.title: Sharing state between components
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Two components, one number

Sometimes two components need the **same** information. A scoreboard shows the score, and the buttons change it. If each one keeps its own state, they don't know about each other: click a button and the scoreboard stays the same!

The fix is called **lifting state up**: move the state into the **parent**, the component that holds them both. Then:

- The parent passes the value **down** as a prop: `<Scoreboard score={score} />`
- The parent passes a **function** down too, so the child can ask for a change: `<Buttons onScore={() => setScore(score + 1)} />`

```jsx
function Buttons(props) {
  return <button onClick={props.onScore}>Goal!</button>;
}
```

The child doesn't change anything itself. It calls the function it was given, the parent changes its state, and React draws **both** children again with the new number.

### New words

- **Parent / child**: if App's JSX has `<Buttons />` in it, App is the parent and Buttons is the child.
- **Lifting state up**: moving state into the parent so its children can share it.
- **Callback prop**: a function passed as a prop, so a child can tell its parent something happened.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: The score lives in `App`. `Scoreboard` gets the score, `GoalButton` gets a function. Click **Goal!** and both stay in step.

lessons.title: Lifting state up
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Where should state live?

State belongs to one component. When two components need the same data (a product list that shows quantities and a cart summary that shows totals), neither one can own it. The rule:

> Put state in the **closest common parent** of every component that uses it.

That's **lifting state up**. The parent owns the state and passes:

- the **data** down as props, so children can render it
- **callback props** (functions) down, so children can ask for changes

```jsx
function App() {
  const [cart, setCart] = useState({});
  const add = (id) => setCart((c) => ({ ...c, [id]: (c[id] ?? 0) + 1 }));
  return (
    <>
      <ProductList cart={cart} onAdd={add} />
      <CartSummary cart={cart} />
    </>
  );
}
```

Data flows **down** through props; events flow **up** through callbacks. Children like `CartSummary` become **presentational**: they don't own anything, they render what they're given, which makes them easy to reuse and test.

### Name callbacks for what happened

By convention, props are `onSomething` (`onAdd`, `onDelete`, `onSelect`), and the parent's functions are `handleSomething` or a verb (`addToCart`). The child says *what happened*; the parent decides *what to do*.

### Updating objects in state

`{ ...c, [id]: newValue }` copies the object and changes one key. `[id]` is a **computed property name**: the key is the *value* of `id`. And `c[id] ?? 0` uses the **nullish coalescing** operator: it falls back to 0 when the product isn't in the cart yet.

### Don't copy props into state

`const [count, setCount] = useState(props.count)` only uses the prop the *first* time; later changes are ignored. If a value comes from the parent, read the prop directly.

### New words

- **Lifting state up**: moving shared state to the closest common parent.
- **Callback prop**: a function prop a child calls to tell the parent something happened.
- **Presentational component**: a component that only renders the props it's given.
- **Computed property name**: `{ [key]: value }`, an object key taken from a variable.
- **Nullish coalescing** (`??`): `a ?? b` gives `b` only when `a` is `null` or `undefined`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: `TabBar` and `TabPanel` are siblings, so the selected tab lives in their parent. `TabBar` reports clicks with `onSelect`; `App` updates the state; both re-render.

lessons.title: Project: Wish list app
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Put it all together

Time to build a whole app by yourself! A wish list uses almost everything from this course:

| You need… | Use… |
| --- | --- |
| To remember what's typed | state + `value` and `onChange` |
| To add a wish when the form is sent | `onSubmit` + `preventDefault` |
| To show all the wishes | `map` with a `key` |
| To remove one wish | `filter` |
| A message when the list is empty | `&&` |

### Removing with filter

`filter` keeps the items you say yes to. To remove one wish, keep every wish **except** that one:

```jsx
setWishes(wishes.filter((wish) => wish.id !== id));
```

`!==` means "is not the same as."

### Give each wish an id

Two wishes could have the same words ("socks", "socks"), and keys must be different. So give each wish an object with an `id` number that goes up by one each time: `{ id: 1, text: "socks" }`.

### Plan first

Before typing, look at the starter and ask: what does this app need to **remember**? Those things become state. Everything else can be worked out from them.

### New words

- **filter**: makes a new array with only the items that pass a test.
- **!==**: "is not equal to."
- **id**: a number or name that's different for every item, so you can find one item exactly.

lessons.title: Project: Task tracker
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Your end-of-course project

You'll build a task tracker the way React developers build real features: plan the state, split the UI into components, then wire them together. It uses everything from this course and the last one.

### 1. Find the minimal state

List everything the UI shows, then ask of each item: *can it be calculated from something else?* If so, it's **derived**, not state.

| The UI shows | State or derived? |
| --- | --- |
| The tasks (title, done) | **State**: `tasks` |
| Which filter is picked | **State**: `filter` |
| The tasks under the current filter | Derived: `tasks.filter(…)` |
| "2 tasks left" | Derived: count of tasks not done |
| What's typed in the new-task box | **State**, but it only matters to the form, so it lives in `TaskForm` |

Keep state as close as possible to where it's used, and lift it only as far as it needs to go.

### 2. Split into components

- `TaskForm` owns its text box and reports new titles with `onAdd(title)`.
- `TaskItem` renders one task and reports clicks with `onToggle(id)`.
- `App` owns `tasks` and `filter`, and does the updates.

### 3. Immutable updates for every action

```jsx
setTasks((ts) => [...ts, newTask]);                                       // add
setTasks((ts) => ts.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t))); // toggle one
setTasks((ts) => ts.filter((t) => !t.done));                              // remove many
```

Each new task needs a stable, unique id. `crypto.randomUUID()` makes one, like `"3b241101-e2bb-4255-8caf-4136c566a962"`.

### 4. Data-driven UI

Instead of writing three filter buttons by hand, describe the filters as data (`FILTERS`) and map over them. Adding a fourth filter is then one line. `Object.entries(obj)` gives you `[key, value]` pairs to map over.

Use `aria-pressed` on toggle-style buttons, so screen readers announce which filter is on; the CSS can style the same attribute.

### New words

- **Minimal state**: the smallest set of values that everything else can be calculated from.
- **Colocation**: keeping state in the component that uses it, lifting only when needed.
- **UUID** (*Universally Unique Identifier*): a long random id that's practically never repeated.
- **Data-driven UI**: rendering from a data description (like an object of filters) instead of repeating JSX.
- **aria-pressed**: tells assistive technology whether a toggle button is on.
